game bird hunters. So firstly, Fish and Game agrees that the
conservation framework needs to be modernized, and we welcome the
move to a more integrated and efficient system.

changes to the Wildlife Act and also consideration of a fish and game
bill on the future horizon.
The points I want to raise today are points we think may not have been fully worked
through as the bill was put together, rather than objections to what the
bill is trying to achieve. And so we're hoping our submission was seen in that
light and that has been helpful. And we look forward to continuing to work,
um, with the government, um, with the Minister for Conservation, and with the
Department of Conservation, um, on, uh, as the planning framework is
established through the National Conservation Policy Statement and
area plans.
Just a couple of points. Angling and game bird hunting value should be
recognized as distinct from recreation.
I set this out in quite a bit of detail within our submission.
This is really important because parts of the proposed changes to the
Conservation Act are significantly,
um, uh, walk across or step across
Fish and Game statutory, current statutory functions, the values of
sports fish and game birds, and our activities on the conservation
estate. And so we think some material changes are really required to
be made through the Amendment Bill to ensure that those statutory
functions are retained and those powers are retained by the organization.
Uh, we're seeking an amendment to Section 6A and Section 6EA
to recognize hunting and fishing values as standalone values, and I set that out in
more detail.
We're not recognized as partners in the new planning framework.
I've a little bit of alluded to that at the beginning.
It doesn't, um, through the framework, it enables the,
uh, Minister for Conservation to make decisions, but there's no requirement to
essentially consult with Fish and Game in relation to our values or the management
of sports fish or game bird, uh, populations through the provisions of the bill.
And this is further weakened by the way that our, our, um,
management plans, our sports fish and game bird management plans are treated by the
amendments through the bill as well.
So they become subservient to the higher level policies within the
Conservation Amendment, um, framework without
recognizing fishing or game bird hunting values as standalone values
in themselves.
The other one that we want to talk about is that our statutory functions shouldn't
require a concession. So we undertake game bird, um, monitoring and
sports fish monitoring within the conservation estate.
Things like electric fishing, um, looking at spawning surveys, and
also management over game bird populations, and we're wanting those to be exempted
from, uh, the requirement to have a concession.
So in closing, we support the bill as it's been set up to do.
Uh, us, a practical refinements that would make the framework work better for our
anglers and our hunters, um, and for the fisheries wetlands and access they depend
upon. And recognizing hunting and fishuring, fishing as distinct values bring
our management plans into the framework and make us a consul tee rather than
as an afterthought, I think will strengthen up the management of their species and
their habitats.

Thank you.

we'll hand over to you to open up and then open for questions.
Thank you. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and members of the committee.
Thank you for providing EDS with this opportunity to present today.
My name is Shaye Schlaefer. I'm EDS's Chief Operating Officer
and General Counsel.
I want to start by saying that EDS is
opposed to the bill in its current form,
but we believe it can be fixed. The bill is
not beyond repair.
We think that amending the bill and panel beating it into
shape would be a better outcome than binning it
altogether.
Conservation law reform is required.
However, we have several big-ticket issues with the bill
that need amendment before we can support it, and these
are outlined in our submission, and I address four of them today.
We've chosen not to focus on exchange and disposals,
because the minister has already said that those provisions
should be pulled. So, the first issue I want
to discuss is the economic opportunities clauses,
and that's new Section 6EA, which has been discussed
a lot with other submitters. But also the corresponding
sections in 13D2,
13H2B, and in Section 14,
relating to the purpose of the National Conservation Policy
Statement, area plans, and the concessions framework.
Our first preference is that these clauses be deleted.
Alternatively, we have provided some acceptable
redrafting in our submission.
Key here is to delete the words "to the greatest
extent practicable,"
and make references to use and development consistent
with conservation.
And I've watched all of the other submitters who have presented to you to
date, and it seems that is a universal request.
Without those changes, the economic clauses place use
and development before conservation.
And that is because DOC functions have no hierarchy
which prioritize conservation imperatives.
The words "to enable use and development to the greatest extent
practical" are an open-ended maximizing
direction,
and because there is no corresponding conservation
direction in those other clauses I just referred to,
to counter the economic purpose of the
conservation policy statement area plans and the
concessions framework.
Cabinet was very clear that economic development was to
be provided only to the extent that it is
consistent with conservation.
We want to make it clear that does not mean balancing
conservation and economic development.
A balancing approach was expressly discounted as an
option by Cabinet.
So we're simply asking the select committee to give effect to Cabinet's
direction to prioritize conservation.
The second issue is with visitor amenity areas.
EDS supports VAA's in principle as
a strategic tool for managing visitors.
However, as drafted, the VAA
framework under the bill is not consistent with
conservation.
And that is reflected in a few different places.
The purpose statement for visitor amenity areas,
the broad list of activities that are provided for,
that visitor amenity areas operate as an override of area
plans, and the conservation purpose for which the land is
held,
that the assessment of VAAs is focused on the parent
land, which has the potential of minimizing impacts that
are actually significant at the estate scale,
and finally, that public input on the development of VAAs is
limited.
So in that context, we have considerable concern with
the minister's decision-making powers for VAAs.
There are simply not enough conservation guardrails to
ensure that the minister's decisions on
VAAs is required to prioritize conservation
values and imperatives.
And we've set out in our submission the amendments that we think are
required to the VAA framework to bring it into an
acceptable position.
The third issue I want to highlight is the centralization of
decision-making power with the minister and the
corresponding reduction in the roles of the Conservation
Authority and conservation boards.
EDS does not think that streamlining the conservation system
requires removing those checks and balances.
The Conservation Authority provides independent
national level expertise and oversight,
and conservation boards bring local knowledge and provide an important
connection between conservation decision making and the
communities that are affected by it.
So under the bill, those roles are significantly diminished while the
minister assumes greater control over conservation management
planning.
And that is particularly concerning when combined with the economic
development imperative and the broad VAA powers that I've just
discussed.
Those changes all pull in the same direction, which is
greater scope for development, coupled with fewer
independent and place-based checks on how those powers are
exercised.
We support streamlining the planning system, but streamlining should mean
removing unnecessary complexity and delay, not removing
conservation guardrails.
We therefore recommend retaining a meaningful decision-making
role for the Conservation Authority and conservation boards
within the new planning framework.
And the final issue I want to address relates to climate change.
So the bill is silent on climate change
considerations, and that has also flowed through into
the conservation policy, the first draft of that.
And we think that is a significant omission for a law that is
intended to provide a new framework for managing the
conservation estate for decades to come.
Climate change is already affecting conservation management.
It's changing where species can survive, it's
increasing pressure on vulnerable ecosystems, and it's
increasing risks to DOC assets and infrastructure.
And I know that one of the members referred to the Cathedral Cove
scenario, which is a prime example of this.
So new planning and concession systems need to be able to
respond to those changes. We recommend that the bill
integrate climate change considerations into the planning and concessions
framework. And again, our submission sets out
how we recommend that occur.
So to sum up, EDS supports reform of the conservation
system. There are real problems with the current system, and there is a
lot in this bill that provides a good foundation for change.
But the fundamental principle of any new conservation law must remain
clear that conservation comes first, and we
don't think that the bill as introduced achieves that.
We're happy to take questions.

electricity generation's existing interaction with public
conservation land. It's not simply whether or not the power
station sits on DOC land. Rather, in practice, it's
much more about the generation scheme's reliance on supporting
infrastructure that sits on, under, over,
or is accessed through public conservation land.
So that might be a tunnel, a canal, a water intake,
an electricity cable, or a communications cable,
geothermal pipeline, monitoring equipment, or
simply an access road or a bridge through public conservation
land. It also includes routine activities needed to
keep a generation scheme operating safely,
access for inspections, maintenance, vegetation management,
and replacing aging equipment.
Those supporting activities generally require some form of
approval from DOC,
usually through the concession system.
Sure.
The scale of that interaction is
significant. The renewable generation assets identified in our
submission, which you'll see on the maps in front of you,
interact with the conservation estate, are associated with around
26,500 gigawatt hours of electricity each year,
about 60% of New Zealand's annual generation.
Wow.
Interesting.

beneath the Rotokawa conservation area
without any surface disturbance on the conservation land.

important link in the operating arrangements needed to keep an
existing generation scheme working safely and reliably.

needed to use it for these supporting activities are
already an important dependency for a significant part of New
Zealand's renewable electricity supply.
That means secure, workable access to public conservation land
is not just an administrative issue for individual generators,

part of New Zealand's electricity system.
